{{about|a growth rate that is exponential in a polylogarithmic function|polynomials with periodically varying coefficients|quasi-polynomial}}
{{Short description|Subexponential bound in computational complexity}}
{{Use mdy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=December 2023}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=December 2023}}
In [[theoretical computer science]], a [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f(n)</math> is said to exhibit '''quasi-polynomial growth''' when it has an [[upper bound]] of the form
<math display=block>f(n)=2^{O\bigl((\log n)^c\bigr)}</math>
for some constant <math>c</math>, as expressed using [[big O notation]]. That is, it is bounded by an [[exponential function]] of a [[polylogarithmic function]]. This generalizes the [[polynomial]]s and the functions of polynomial growth, for which one can take <math>c=1</math>. A function with quasi-polynomial growth is also said to be '''quasi-polynomially bounded'''.{{r|pareto}}

Quasi-polynomial growth has been used in the [[analysis of algorithms]] to describe certain algorithms whose [[computational complexity]] is not polynomial, but is substantially smaller than [[exponential growth|exponential]]. In particular, algorithms whose [[worst-case analysis|worst-case running time]]s exhibit quasi-polynomial growth are said to take [[quasi-polynomial time]].{{r|vzg}} As well as [[time complexity]], some algorithms require quasi-polynomial [[space complexity]],{{r|space}} use a quasi-polynomial number of parallel processors,{{r|qnc}} can be expressed as algebraic formulas of quasi-polynomial size{{r|vzg}} or have a quasi-polynomial [[competitive ratio]].{{r|online}} In some other cases, quasi-polynomial growth is used to model restrictions on the inputs to a problem that, when present, lead to good performance from algorithms on those inputs.{{r|pareto}} It can also bound the size of the output for some problems; for instance, for the [[shortest path problem]] with linearly varying edge weights, the number of distinct solutions can be quasipolynomial.{{r|carstensen|bfp}}

Beyond theoretical computer science, quasi-polynomial growth bounds have also been used in mathematics, for instance in partial results on the [[Hirsch conjecture]] for the diameter of polytopes in [[polyhedral combinatorics]],{{r|diam}} or relating the sizes of [[clique (graph theory)|cliques]] and [[independent set (graph theory)|independent sets]] in certain classes of graphs.{{r|quasiX}} However, in polyhedral combinatorics and [[enumerative combinatorics]], a different meaning of the same word also is used, for the [[quasi-polynomial]]s, functions that generalize polynomials by having periodic coefficients.{{r|ehrhart}}
